summary: As emerging quantum architectures evolve into heterogeneous networks combining different physical substrates, such as qubits for logic and higher-dimensional qudits for robust communication, the traditional scalar metrics of quantum error correction become insufficient. To address this, we introduce a mathematical framework based on dimension multisets to characterize quantum error-correcting codes (QECC) and absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states in mixed-dimensional Hilbert spaces. By replacing scalar weights with multisets, we accurately capture the exact physical composition of error supports across these diverse systems. Our central result is the mixed-dimensional quantum MacWilliams identity, which establishes the formal algebraic relationship between Shor-Laflamme enumerators and unitary weight enumerators. From this foundation, we deduce the mixed-dimensional shadow identity and derive rigorous, generalized constraints on code parameters, explicitly formulating the mixed-dimensional quantum Hamming, Singleton and Scott bounds, and developing a linear program to systematically evaluate code viability. For the Singleton bound, a tighter bound that has no homogeneous analogue is derived for pure mixed-dimensional codes. Finally, we deploy this enumerator machinery to thoroughly analyze AME states, utilizing shadow inequalities to constrain their existence and introducing a combinatorial grid method for the explicit construction of mixed-dimensional tripartite AME states.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a mathematical framework for characterizing quantum error-correcting codes and maximally entangled states in mixed-dimensional Hilbert spaces, utilizing multisets to enhance traditional quantum metrics.
AI.motivation: To advance quantum error correction in heterogeneous networks with mixed-dimensional qubits and qudits. Traditional scalar metrics have proven inadequate.
AI.method: Introducing dimension multisets to replace scalar weights for describing quantum error-correcting codes and their error supports; formulating mixed-dimensional quantum MacWilliams identity and bounds for code parameters.
AI.result: Development of the mixed-dimensional shadow identity and generalized constraints, including new bounds for pure mixed-dimensional codes and application of enumerator machinery to analyze AME states.
AI.conclusion: The framework allows for systematic evaluation and construction of mixed-dimensional quantum codes and AME states, with new insights into their existence and properties.

title: Pseudo-Hermiticity of the Nakajima-Zwanzig Projected Liouvillian in the Jaynes-Cummings Model
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Supplemental Material included (2 pages)
summary: The Nakajima-Zwanzig projected Liouvillian QLQ, the generator of the exact memory kernel in open quantum dynamics, is manifestly non-Hermitian yet has been reported to possess a purely real spectrum in the Jaynes-Cummings model -- an anomaly unexplained since observation. We resolve this anomaly by showing that QLQ is pseudo-Hermitian in the Mostafazadeh sense: a positive-definite metric eta>0 exists such that (QLQ)^dag eta = eta (QLQ), forcing the spectrum to be real. The pseudo-Hermiticity is genuine: the Delta N = 0 and Delta N = +/-2 sectors are individually non-Hermitian (residuals 1.70 and 5.06, respectively), yet the global spectrum is protected by eta. The metric survives the bath-truncation limit (N_max = 3--20, matrix dimension up to 1764 x 1764) with intertwining residual <10^{-11}. A continuous deformation to the full Rabi model reveals a re-entrant pseudo-Hermitian phase with two exceptional-point boundaries, in which the metric condition number diverges. The result supplies a structural reason for Hardy-space analyticity of the memory kernel in the canonical quantum-optical model.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves an anomaly in the non-Hermitian Nakajima-Zwanzig projected Liouvillian QLQ, showing it is pseudo-Hermitian with a real spectrum due to a positive-definite metric.
AI.motivation: The study addresses the unexplained anomaly of QLQ having a real spectrum despite being manifestly non-Hermitian in the Jaynes-Cummings model.
AI.method: Demonstrates that QLQ is pseudo-Hermitian by identifying a positive-definite metric that satisfies the condition (QLQ)†η = η(QLQ), ensuring real eigenvalues.
AI.result: The metric is shown to remain stable across bath-truncation limits, and a continuous deformation to the Rabi model reveals a re-entrant pseudo-Hermitian phase.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a structural justification for the analyticity of the memory kernel in canonical quantum optics.

title: Proof of the Error Scaling for Universally Robust Dynamical Decoupling Sequences
summary: Universally robust dynamical decoupling (UR$n$) sequences were proposed to compensate pulse imperfections arising from arbitrary experimental parameters while achieving high-order error suppression with only a linear increase in the number of pulses. Although their performance was supported by analytical arguments, numerical simulations, and experiments, a complete mathematical proof of the claimed order of error compensation has been absent. In this work, we present a rigorous proof for UR$n$ DD sequences with even $n$. Using a series expansion of a quantity whose modulus is the fidelity $F$, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the cancellation of its coefficients up to, but not including, order $n$. The UR$n$ phase prescription satisfies these conditions, and therefore $1-F=O(ε^n)$. Our results establish the UR$n$ construction on firm analytical grounds and clarify the structure responsible for its high-order robustness.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a rigorous mathematical proof for the performance of Universally Robust dynamical decoupling (UR$n$) sequences, confirming their claimed error suppression capabilities and enhancing understanding of their robustness.
AI.motivation: To address the lack of a complete mathematical proof for the effectiveness of UR$n$ sequences in error suppression due to pulse imperfections.
AI.method: Utilizing a series expansion of fidelity and deriving conditions for the cancellation of coefficients up to order $n$, we show that the UR$n$ phase prescription meets these conditions.
AI.result: The proof confirms that the error 1-F is of order $O(ε^n)$, validating the UR$n$ sequences' robustness against arbitrary pulse imperfections.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a solid analytical foundation for UR$n$ sequences and elucidates the mechanisms behind their high-order error compensation.

title: A Quantum Spectral Framework for Solving PDEs
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental across numerous scientific fields. As these problems scale to high dimensions, classical numerical schemes introduce severe computational bottlenecks, known as the curse of dimensionality. Attempts to solve this problem typically rely on either classical sparsity and low-rank decompositions, or neural network surrogate models. On the other hand, Quantum Computing offers a promising alternative, as it allows us to operate in significantly larger spaces while demanding far fewer resources. In this work, we present a quantum subroutine to solve second-order linear PDEs by exploiting the structural properties of the filter in Fourier space using Quantum Block Encoding (QBE) with quantum reversible arithmetic. This approach serves as a specialized alternative to standard quantum matrix inversion, which typically relies solely on Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) without exploiting the inherent structural properties of the matrix. We validate the proposed methodology against its classical counterpart to prove its correctness. This framework provides a foundation for extending these methods toward quantum group Fourier transforms, wavelet-based analysis, and equivariant quantum neural networks (EQNNs), offering a promising path toward solving broader classes of problems, including nonlinear PDEs.

AI.tldr: A quantum subroutine is proposed to solve second-order linear PDEs efficiently using Quantum Block Encoding, overcoming limitations of traditional methods in high-dimensional spaces.
AI.motivation: Classical numerical schemes struggle with high-dimensional PDEs due to the curse of dimensionality, necessitating exploration of alternatives like quantum computing.
AI.method: The proposed method employs Quantum Block Encoding and reversible arithmetic to exploit the structure of filters in Fourier space, enhancing matrix inversion processes beyond current quantum techniques.
AI.result: The methodology is validated against classical methods, showing correctness and promising efficiency improvements in solving second-order linear PDEs.
AI.conclusion: This work lays the groundwork for future applications in quantum Fourier transforms, wavelet analysis, and potentially nonlinear PDEs, demonstrating the versatility of quantum approaches in computational science.

title: Quantum channels preserving sigma-additivity and Ulam measurable cardinals
summary:
This paper investigates the interplay between the properties of quantum states on the Hilbert space \(\ell_2(κ)\) and the set-theoretic nature of the cardinal $κ$.
  We focus on the existence of singular $σ$-additive states~ -- functionals whose induced measures are $σ$-additive yet vanish on singletons.
  While the existence of such states is known to be equivalent to the Ulam measurability of $κ$, their structural and dynamical properties remain largely unexplored.
  We prove that any $σ$-additive state on the diagonal algebra is representable as a Pettis integral over a singular $σ$-additive measure, extending the classical representation theory to the non-normal sector.
  Furthermore, we construct a class of quantum channels using $σ$-complete ultrafilters that map normal states to singular $σ$-additive states, effectively <<archiving>> information into the singular part of the state space.

AI.tldr: This paper explores singular σ-additive states in quantum mechanics, relating them to the cardinality of sets and providing structural insights into their representation and application in quantum channels.
AI.motivation: To understand the properties and implications of singular σ-additive states in quantum physics, particularly their connection to Ulam measurability and set theory.
AI.method: The authors establish that any σ-additive state can be represented as a Pettis integral over a singular σ-additive measure, and they design quantum channels using σ-complete ultrafilters that transform normal states into singular σ-additive states.
AI.result: The paper elucidates the structural representation of σ-additive states and introduces a new class of quantum channels capable of encoding information into the singular component of the state space.
AI.conclusion: The findings extend classical representation theory to a broader context in quantum mechanics, highlighting the significance of singular σ-additive states and their practical applications.

title: Minimum Toffoli depth for the multi-controlled Toffoli gate via teleportation
summary: The decomposition of complex quantum operations into experimentally feasible gate sets has been a central challenge since the early development of quantum computing. The multi-controlled Toffoli (MCT) gate is a key example, with applications across a wide range of quantum algorithms, whose decomposition into smaller gates, however, typically leads to deep circuits. In this work, we introduce a teleportation-based decomposition that implements an arbitrary MCT gate with unit Toffoli depth, independent of the number of controls, while maintaining a relatively low Toffoli count compared to existing approaches. This is achieved at the cost of a linear overhead in ancilla qubits and the ability to distribute entangled pairs across distant qubits, a capability already available in several quantum computing platforms. We further demonstrate the advantages of this implementation in circuits that rely on MCT gates, such as the adder operator, quantum read-only memory, quantum neurons, and quantum decision trees.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a teleportation-based decomposition for multi-controlled Toffoli gates, achieving unit Toffoli depth and lower gate count, while requiring additional ancilla qubits.
AI.motivation: Decomposing complex quantum operations into practical gate sets is essential for advancing quantum computing, particularly for efficient use of multi-controlled Toffoli gates in quantum algorithms.
AI.method: A teleportation-based approach that allows for the implementation of an arbitrary multi-controlled Toffoli gate with unit depth and fewer gates using ancilla qubits.
AI.result: The proposed decomposition method maintains low gate count and unit depth, improving the performance of circuits relying on MCT gates over existing techniques.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that this decomposition is advantageous for various quantum circuits, enabling more efficient quantum computations in platforms that can manage entangled states.

title: MCMit: Mid-Circuit Measurement Error Mitigation
summary:
Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) and Quantum Error Correction (QEC) rely on dynamic circuits that include Mid-Circuit Measurements (MCMs) and classical feedback. These operations present a major bottleneck: MCMs suffer from high error rates that lead to real-time branching errors, while MCM and classical feedback latencies amplify decoherence errors. Current hardware controllers, qubit-state discriminators, and software error mitigation techniques fail to address these challenges holistically.
  We propose MCMit, a hardware-software co-design to mitigate branching and latency-induced errors. MCMit introduces a scalable, constant-latency multi-control branch instruction for faster classical feedback and two qubit-state discriminators, a transformer, and a CNN, with high accuracy even under short measurement durations. On the software side, static MCM elimination and stochastic branching complement the hardware by mitigating residual branching errors that persist despite hardware improvements.
  We implement MCMit on Qubic and evaluate it using experimentally extracted QPU readout traces. Our branch instruction reduces feedback latency by up to 70\%, improving circuit depths by up to $7\times$ over Qubic. Our CNN discriminator achieves 37-73\% higher accuracy for short measurement durations than the baselines, leading to up to 80\% lower logical error rates in QEC. Last, our software mitigation improves fidelity by 18--30\% over baseline methods.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MCMit, a co-designed hardware-software solution addressing the challenges of Mid-Circuit Measurements and classical feedback in Distributed Quantum Computing, significantly reducing error rates and improving circuit performance.
AI.motivation: The high error rates and latencies associated with Mid-Circuit Measurements in Quantum Computing hinder the efficiency of Quantum Error Correction and the overall performance of DQC.
AI.method: MCMit integrates a multi-control branch instruction and employs two types of qubit-state discriminators (a transformer and a CNN), alongside software improvements like static MCM elimination and stochastic branching to reduce errors.
AI.result: The proposed method reduces feedback latency by up to 70%, increases circuit depths by up to 7 times, and improves discrimination accuracy by 37-73%, resulting in up to 80% lower logical error rates in Quantum Error Correction.
AI.conclusion: MCMit demonstrates significant enhancements in the fidelity and performance of quantum circuits, validating its effectiveness compared to baseline methods.

title: Quantum limit cycles with continuous symmetries from coherent parametric driving: exact solutions and many-body extensions
summary: There is widespread interest in many-body quantum systems that exhibit limit-cycle or time-crystalline behaviour. An ideal quantum limit cycle would be realized using fully coherent driving (to minimize noise) and also have a continuous internal symmetry (to ensure generation of monochromatic radiation). While these two requirements may seem incompatible, we introduce in this work a large class of multi-mode bosonic limit cycle models based on coherent parametric driving which possess an O(N) continuous symmetry. Surprisingly, the full quantum dissipative steady state of these models can be found exactly. They exhibit rich physics, including steady state entanglement, reduced phase diffusion and the possibility of realizing quantum limit tori. The basic mechanism we identify provides a unified way to understand how coherent parametric driving can yield symmetry-enriched limit cycles, and also helps us understand related models where the relevant symmetries are weakly broken. The models we study are compatible with a range of different experimental platforms, including quantum optical setups and superconducting quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a class of multi-mode bosonic models exhibiting limit-cycle behavior, achievable through coherent parametric driving while maintaining continuous internal symmetry, leading to exact solutions for their quantum dissipative steady states.
AI.motivation: The research addresses the challenge of achieving limit-cycle behavior in many-body quantum systems using coherent driving and continuous symmetry, two seemingly incompatible requirements.
AI.method: The authors introduce multi-mode bosonic limit cycle models driven by coherent parametric methods, establishing conditions under which an O(N) continuous symmetry exists and deriving exact solutions for their full quantum dissipative steady states.
AI.result: The models reveal phenomena such as steady state entanglement, reduced phase diffusion, and the potential for quantum limit tori, all while being compatible with various experimental platforms.
AI.conclusion: The study provides insights into the mechanisms behind coherent parametric driving and its role in yielding symmetry-enriched limit cycles, enhancing understanding of related quantum systems where symmetries may be weakly broken.

title: QCalEval: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Quantum Calibration Plot Understanding
summary: Quantum computing calibration depends on interpreting experimental data, and calibration plots provide the most universal human-readable representation for this task, yet no systematic evaluation exists of how well vision-language models (VLMs) interpret them. We introduce QCalEval, the first VLM benchmark for quantum calibration plots: 243 samples across 87 scenario types from 22 experiment families, spanning superconducting qubits and neutral atoms, evaluated on six question types in both zero-shot and in-context learning settings. The best general-purpose zero-shot model reaches a mean score of 72.3, and many open-weight models degrade under multi-image in-context learning, whereas frontier closed models improve substantially. A supervised fine-tuning ablation at the 9-billion-parameter scale shows that SFT improves zero-shot performance but cannot close the multimodal in-context learning gap. As a reference case study, we release NVIDIA Ising Calibration 1, an open-weight model based on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B that reaches 74.7 zero-shot average score.

AI.tldr: QCalEval introduces a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on quantum calibration plots, revealing performance discrepancies among models in zero-shot and in-context learning settings.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate how well vision-language models interpret quantum calibration plots, which are essential for quantum computing calibration.
AI.method: The study introduces QCalEval, a benchmark consisting of 243 samples and 87 scenario types assessed against six question types in zero-shot and in-context learning settings.
AI.result: The best zero-shot model achieved a mean score of 72.3, while closed models improved under in-context learning, and a supervised fine-tuning at the 9-billion-parameter scale enhanced zero-shot performance but didn't resolve in-context learning gaps.
AI.conclusion: The QCalEval benchmark reveals distinct performance trends among various models, emphasizing the potential of supervised fine-tuning and the need for continued exploration in multimodal learning for better calibration interpretation.

title: Testing a continuous-variable Bell-like inequality with a hybrid-encoded system
summary: Continuous-variable quantum systems are promising candidates for quantum computing and quantum information processing. It is widely known that quadrature measurements on Gaussian continuous-variable systems can be described by a noncontextual hidden-variable model and cannot violate a Bell inequality. Here, we demonstrate that the observation fails when sequential measurements are involved. Our experiment is realized by mapping the spatial modes of a single photon, deterministically generated from an InAs/GaAs quantum emitter, to the logical operations in the Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill code space. Employing a black-box-style approach, we observe a violation of the Bell-like noncontextual hidden-variable inequality by 380 standard deviations. Our results address the conceptual loopholes in previous works and open up new possibilities for studying fundamental quantum physics using photonic-encoded continuous-variable systems.

AI.tldr: The study demonstrates that sequential measurements in continuous-variable quantum systems can violate Bell inequalities, providing new insights into quantum mechanics and expanding the potential of photonic-encoded systems.
AI.motivation: To explore the limitations of noncontextual hidden-variable models in continuous-variable systems during sequential measurements.
AI.method: The experiment involved mapping spatial modes of a photon from an InAs/GaAs quantum emitter to operations in the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill code, utilizing a black-box approach to assess measurement outcomes.
AI.result: A violation of the Bell-like noncontextual hidden-variable inequality was observed by 380 standard deviations, indicating that sequential measurements can challenge previously held beliefs.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal conceptual loopholes in prior research, paving the way for further investigations in fundamental quantum physics with photonic continuous-variable systems.

title: Heralding probability optimization for nonclassical light generated by photon counting measurements on multimode Gaussian states
summary: Generation of highly non-classical quantum states of light is essential for optical quantum information processing and quantum metrology. Given the lack of sufficiently strong nonlinear interactions between optical fields, the commonly employed optical quantum-state preparation schemes are conditional, based on nonlinearity induced by heralding photon number measurement on a part of a multimode squeezed Gaussian state. Development and optimization of such probabilistic quantum-state engineering schemes represents one of the central challenges in current quantum optics. As technology advances and experiments progress to detection of higher numbers of photons, the maximization of the heralding probability becomes essential to ensure sufficiently high state-preparation rates. Here, we show that for the conditional quantum state preparation schemes based on Gaussian states and photon number measurements the maximization of the heralding probability can be formulated as finding solution to a system of polynomial equations, which offers an efficient way to find the optimal configuration and allows us to apply techniques dedicated specifically to solving such systems of equations. Our approach can seamlessly incorporate bounds on the available single-mode quadrature squeezing, which is highly experimentally relevant. We mainly consider generation of finite superpositions of Fock states but show that the approach can be straightforwardly extended to generation of squeezed superpositions of Fock states. We focus on Gaussian states with vanishing coherent displacements, hence the conditionally generated states have well defined photon number parity. We illustrate our general methodology on examples of generation of single-mode and two-mode states with two heralding modes.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the optimization of conditional quantum state preparation schemes for generating non-classical states of light, emphasizing the maximization of heralding probability via polynomial equations.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the need for efficient optical quantum state preparation schemes, which are crucial for advancements in quantum information processing and metrology, particularly when experimental capabilities increase.
AI.method: The authors present a method to maximize heralding probability by formulating it as a problem of solving polynomial equations, incorporating experimental constraints on single-mode quadrature squeezing.
AI.result: They demonstrate that their approach effectively identifies optimal configurations for generating finite superpositions of Fock states and can be adapted for squeezed superpositions.
AI.conclusion: This methodology can streamline quantum state preparation, allowing for higher state-preparation rates and advancing experimental applications in quantum optics.
